findings.issue: Line 7 requires a sibling paper repository, but line 35 still permits an absolute path to reuse a project elsewhere. The initializer likewise accepts destinations outside the sibling layout. An agent receives contradictory location instructions.

# Independent Paper Projects

Use this guide when entering, resuming or relocating a paper project, or maintaining its material links. Once located, write there without repeating discovery or initialization. A standalone revision, discussion or search needs no repository.

## Locate before creating

Check the author's explicit path, the known paper project, then sibling candidates and explicit manuscript links. From a code subdirectory, find its root with `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`. Inspect directory names, Git ownership and necessary project descriptions, without recursively searching code or experiments. A directory name alone does not establish an occupied directory's identity.

Default location: `<code-root>/../<paper_slug>/`, with independent Git. Preserve the author's established slug; ask if unknown instead of deriving `<code-name>-paper`. Ask about multiple candidates, unrelated occupants or uncertain Git ownership before writes.

Reuse an independent paper directory and its conventions; initialize missing Git in place outside other repositories. Migrate identified legacy manuscripts inside code directly to the sibling paper directory, without asking whether to retain the coupled layout. Move manuscripts, bibliography, formal figures and necessary build files; leave research source documents and unrelated files in code. Identify this file set in mixed directories. Check real paths and collisions first; ask only about unresolved ownership, file selection or conflicts, without overwriting either copy. Preserve a standalone paper's own `.git` when moving its whole repository; never transfer code Git metadata or worktree/submodule indirection. Resolve linked Git registrations before completing migration.

Preserve edits, rebase README materials against their original targets, repair asset/build paths and update explicit links to the moved manuscript. Leave no old working copy, redirect stub or compatibility symlink. Report remaining locations after migration errors instead of continuing in the old layout. Initialize missing starter files after moving to avoid generated-file collisions.

## Keep material links in the paper README

At entry or resume, read the paper-root `README.md` and its `研究材料` section (or existing equivalent). From a paper subdirectory, locate the root first. Resolve links relative to the README's directory, not the current directory. Reuse a mapping already in context; reread the README when links change or become uncertain.

Use ordinary Markdown: a code-project link for location, and named document links with necessary writing purposes. Registered documents are continuing author inputs; read across directories without asking again. The code directory link does not authorize scanning. Fenced/commented examples and unrelated links are not registrations. The [README section template](../assets/templates/paper_readme.md) is illustrative; never register its example paths as real materials.

Select only task-relevant entries: algorithm documents for algorithms, result summaries for Results. Read current contents for each new edit request; reuse content already read for this task unless changed. Do not preload everything or follow links into implementation or experiment audits. Ask about missing scientific definitions instead of guessing engineering labels or investigating code.

Add newly designated project materials or update explicitly replaced entries in place. Resolve supplied paths from their stated context before making them README-relative. Preserve unrelated content and entries; reuse an equivalent section. One-time materials apply now but neither register nor replace persistent entries. Do not invent links for text with no file location. Explicit author corrections/replacements take precedence; otherwise ask about conflicts instead of selecting by filename or modification time. Add no status, date, version or approval fields.

For broken or inaccessible links, ask for a correct, accessible location. For conflicts or necessary missing definitions, pause the dependent passage and ask specifically. File availability does not establish whether research was performed; keep questions outside the manuscript.

## Initialize the minimum

After resolving the destination, run the helper without reading its implementation. Relative destinations use the actual code root's parent even when `--code-root` names a subdirectory. Absolute destinations can reuse projects elsewhere outside other repositories.

```bash
python "<skill-root>/scripts/init_paper_project.py" "<paper_slug>" --code-root "<code-root>"
```

The helper creates independent Git, `README.md` and `.gitignore`, preserving existing files. Its README includes only the real code location; add document links when designated. It does not choose slugs, migrate, parse material lists, commit or configure remotes. Use existing file tools for reading, local README edits and migration, without a parser or sync service. Initialize with exclusive destination access; resolve failures before retrying.

Do not precreate manuscript sections, a venue template, evidence ledgers, or reading collections. Add the actual manuscript, bibliography, and final figures or tables as writing needs them. Use [workspace.md](workspace.md) only for requested auxiliary artifacts.

## Write and share from the paper repository

Resolve edits and Git operations against the paper root. Keep its manuscript format and build conventions. Express registered materials as scientific prose, formal algorithms and final figures in the paper, preserving scientific meaning when replacing engineering labels. Reading and building the formal paper must use paper-local files, without absolute local paths or symlinks into code. The README's external materials support authoring, not the paper build. Keep formal figures trackable; do not mirror code or experiment archives.


# Direct Academic Prose

## Remove defensive writing

Missing material is an author question, not manuscript content. If it prevents writing the requested claim, pause that passage and ask for the specific result, method detail, or intended source. Do not fill it with statements about unavailable materials, unverified results, or what the research supposedly did not do. If the missing material is irrelevant to the passage, leave it out and write the requested text. A limitation explicitly established by the author or source remains a research fact and may belong in the paper.

State the strongest supported proposition at its actual scope. Do not weaken an observed result to make it harder to challenge. For style-only edits, preserve its epistemic strength.

Put necessary scope inside the claim. Remove disclaimers about claims the paper never makes, hypothetical confounder lists, and repeated qualifications. Retain a boundary wherever omitting it would change the interpretation, including in an independently read abstract or conclusion.

Preserve real uncertainty and tradeoffs. When a defensive sentence also contains a relevant interpretive consequence, express that consequence directly rather than deleting the whole sentence. Remove a contrast only when it denies an unmade claim; do not mechanically ban contrast words or erase a measured disadvantage. A proposed explanation may remain an explicitly identified interpretation, without being promoted to a demonstrated mechanism.

- Defensive: `The method outperforms the baseline on both evaluated datasets. However, this does not imply superiority on every possible dataset.`
- Direct: `The method outperforms the baseline on both evaluated datasets.`
- Material boundary: `The estimated reduction was positive, but its confidence interval included zero.`

## Make the evidence carry the paragraph

Lead a results paragraph with the finding that matters to the argument. Select the values and comparisons that establish it, then explain the consequence when it adds information. Do not append a paraphrase of the finding as a substitute for interpretation or force this into a fixed sentence template.

Use figure and table references where they support that reasoning. Combine visuals answering the same question; remove body text that merely repeats a caption. Keep a visual-led sentence when it introduces organization needed to read the analysis.

Explain method choices through the research need and the operation that addresses it. Avoid retrospective justifications invented to make every implementation choice sound like a contribution.

Do not put source-code intermediate variables, internal module aliases, configuration keys, CLI flags, paths, run/job IDs, branches, or workflow metadata into manuscript prose, even as quoted tokens or generic phrases such as "the recorded run." Express the supplied scientific objects, operations, settings, and values directly. Mathematical notation defined for the paper and established scientific method names are distinct from implementation identifiers. If a necessary internal label has no supplied scientific meaning, stop that passage and ask the author; do not guess its expansion or inspect the repository to avoid asking.

# Adaptive Calibration

Author introduction to preserve.

## Algorithm

The algorithm maps an unordered, variable-length set of patch embeddings to a classification output. Given embeddings \(x_1,\ldots,x_n \in \mathbb{R}^{d}\), a learned linear projection assigns each embedding a scalar score \(s_i = w^\top x_i\). Softmax normalization produces weights
\[
\alpha_i = \frac{\exp(s_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\exp(s_j)}.
\]
The algorithm forms the pooled representation \(z = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i x_i\) and passes it to a classifier. Applying the same scoring function to every embedding and aggregating by a weighted sum makes the pooled representation invariant to the order of the input embeddings.

# Adaptive Calibration

Author introduction to preserve.

## Algorithm

The algorithm maps an unordered, variable-length set of patch embeddings to a classification output. Given embeddings \(x_1,\ldots,x_n \in \mathbb{R}^{d}\), a shared two-layer multilayer perceptron \(g_\theta\) assigns each embedding a scalar score \(s_i = g_\theta(x_i)\). Softmax normalization produces weights
\[
\alpha_i = \frac{\exp(s_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\exp(s_j)}.

# Adaptive Calibration

Author introduction to preserve.

## Algorithm

The algorithm classifies an unordered, variable-length set of patch embeddings by aggregating them into a fixed-dimensional representation. Let the input embeddings be \(\{\mathbf{x}_i\}_{i=1}^{n}\), where \(\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d}\) and \(n\) may vary between inputs. A shared learned linear projection assigns a scalar score to each embedding:

\[
s_i = \mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}_i.
\]

The scores are normalized across the input set using softmax, and the resulting weights define the aggregate representation:

\[
\alpha_i = \frac{\exp(s_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{n}\exp(s_j)},
\qquad
\mathbf{z} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i\mathbf{x}_i.
\]

A classifier maps \(\mathbf{z}\) to the predicted class. The aggregate retains dimension \(d\) as the number of patches varies. Reordering the embeddings reorders their scores and weights together, leaving the weighted sum unchanged. Thus, the aggregate representation is permutation invariant.

# Adaptive Calibration

Author introduction to preserve.

## Algorithm

The algorithm maps an unordered, variable-length set of patch embeddings to a prediction through learned weighted aggregation. Let \(X = \{\mathbf{x}_i\}_{i=1}^{N}\), where \(N \geq 1\) and \(\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d}\). A learned linear projection assigns a scalar score to each embedding, and a softmax over the set converts these scores into normalized weights:

\[
s_i = \mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}_i,
\qquad
\alpha_i = \frac{\exp(s_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\exp(s_j)}.
\]

The algorithm then computes the weighted representation

\[
\mathbf{z} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\alpha_i\mathbf{x}_i
\]

and passes \(\mathbf{z}\) to a classifier. This aggregation produces a representation in \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\) regardless of the number of input embeddings, allowing the classifier to operate on sets of varying size.

The weighted representation is permutation invariant: reordering the embeddings reorders their scores and weights together, leaving the softmax denominator and weighted sum unchanged. The classifier therefore receives the same representation for any ordering of a given input set.

Algorithm: input is an unordered variable-length set of patch embeddings. Score each embedding with a learned linear projection, normalize the scores with softmax, compute the weighted sum, then classify it. The weighted sum is permutation invariant. Internal working alias POOL_X7; vector name tmp_vec2. These names are not scientific terminology.

# Adaptive Calibration

Author introduction to preserve.

## Algorithm

The algorithm maps an unordered, variable-length set of patch embeddings to a prediction through learned weighted aggregation. Let \(X = \{\mathbf{x}_i\}_{i=1}^{N}\), where \(N \geq 1\) and \(\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d}\). A learned linear projection assigns a scalar score to each embedding, and a softmax over the set converts these scores into normalized weights:

\[
s_i = \mathbf{w}^{\top}\mathbf{x}_i,
\qquad
\alpha_i = \frac{\exp(s_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\exp(s_j)}.
\]

The algorithm then computes the weighted representation

\[
\mathbf{z} = \sum_{i=1}^{N}\alpha_i\mathbf{x}_i
\]

and passes \(\mathbf{z}\) to a classifier. This aggregation produces a representation in \(\mathbb{R}^{d}\) regardless of the number of input embeddings, allowing the classifier to operate on sets of varying size.

The weighted representation is permutation invariant: reordering the embeddings reorders their scores and weights together, leaving the softmax denominator and weighted sum unchanged. The classifier therefore receives the same representation for any ordering of a given input set.
